os-process-thread:0.prompt: A running process issues a blocking disk read. Which state transition happens?
options: Running → Ready (it gives the CPU back but stays runnable)
Running → Waiting
Running → Terminated
Ready → Running
os-process-thread:0.explanation: A process that must wait for an event (I/O completion) moves to Waiting/Blocked and the CPU goes to another process. Running → Ready happens on preemption, when the process could still run but loses the CPU.

os-process-thread:0.prompt: The disk read that a blocked process was waiting for completes. Where does the process go next?
options: Directly to Running, because I/O completion preempts the current task
To Ready, until the scheduler picks it
To Terminated
Back to New
os-process-thread:0.explanation: I/O completion makes the process runnable, so it joins the ready queue; the scheduler decides when it actually runs. Jumping straight to Running would bypass the scheduler, though some kernels may preempt in favour of the woken task immediately.

os-process-thread:0.prompt: Which of these is NOT typically stored in a process control block (PCB)?
options: Process id and state
Saved program counter and CPU registers
Memory-management info such as page-table pointers
The source code of the program
os-process-thread:0.explanation: The PCB holds what the kernel needs to manage and resume the process: id, state, saved registers and PC, memory mappings, open files, scheduling info and accounting. Source code isn't part of a running process at all; only the loaded machine code is mapped into memory.

os-process-thread:0.prompt: `ps` shows many processes in state Z (defunct) under your Node parent process. What does this mean?
options: They're spinning at 100% CPU
They exited but the parent never called wait()
They have been swapped out to disk because memory is under pressure
They are blocked waiting on network I/O
os-process-thread:0.explanation: A zombie has finished and freed its memory but keeps its PID and exit status until the parent reaps it. Too many zombies can exhaust PIDs. Fix the parent to handle child exit (Node does this for child_process children it spawned).

os-process-thread:0.prompt: A Node app runs as PID 1 in a Docker container and spawns shell scripts that spawn their own children. Zombies accumulate and `docker stop` takes 10 seconds. What's the standard fix?
options: Increase the container's memory limit so zombies have room
Run an init like tini (`docker run --init`)
Use `kill -9` inside the app
Run Node with --max-old-space-size so the heap is capped below the limit
os-process-thread:0.explanation: PID 1 inherits orphaned processes and must reap them, and it gets no default signal handlers, so SIGTERM is ignored unless handled and Docker waits before sending SIGKILL. A tiny init like tini handles both jobs.

os-process-thread:0.prompt: A parent process exits while its child is still running. What happens to the child on Linux?
options: It is killed immediately along with the parent
It's re-parented to init (PID 1) or a subreaper
It becomes a zombie forever
It freezes until the parent restarts and re-attaches to it
os-process-thread:0.explanation: Orphans keep running and are adopted by init (or a process marked as a child subreaper), which later reaps them. They are only killed if something sends them a signal, e.g. when the terminal session ends.

os-process-thread:0.prompt: `top` shows a process in state D for minutes, and `kill -9` doesn't remove it. What does D mean?
options: Dead: the process has exited and is waiting to be removed
Uninterruptible sleep, usually stuck on I/O
Debugging mode
Daemon process detached from any terminal session
os-process-thread:0.explanation: D is uninterruptible sleep: the task is in a kernel path that can't be interrupted by signals until the I/O completes, so even SIGKILL waits. Long D states point to storage or network-filesystem problems.

os-process-thread:0.prompt: Which state transitions are valid in the classic five-state process model? Select all that apply.
options: New → Ready
Ready → Running
Waiting → Running
Running → Ready
Terminated → Ready
os-process-thread:0.explanation: Admitted processes become Ready, the scheduler dispatches Ready → Running, and preemption sends Running → Ready. Waiting processes go to Ready (not directly to Running) when their event occurs, and terminated processes never come back.

os-process-thread:0.prompt: During a context switch between two processes, which information is saved to or loaded from their PCBs? Select all that apply.
options: Program counter
General-purpose CPU registers
Pointer to the page tables (address-space info)
The entire contents of the process heap
Process state
os-process-thread:0.explanation: The kernel saves the outgoing CPU context, updates state, and loads the incoming process's registers and address-space pointer. Heap memory stays where it is; switching page tables changes which memory is visible without copying anything.

os-process-thread:0.prompt: A zombie process still holds its full memory (heap and stack) until its parent calls wait().
options: True
False
os-process-thread:0.explanation: False. On exit the kernel frees the process's memory and most resources; only a small process-table entry with the PID and exit status remains for the parent to collect.

os-process-thread:0.prompt: A process moves from Running to Ready when its time slice expires on a preemptive scheduler.
options: True
False
os-process-thread:0.explanation: True. The timer interrupt preempts it; it's still able to run, so it goes back to the ready queue rather than to Waiting, which is only for processes blocked on an event.

os-process-thread:1.prompt: In the N:1 (many-to-one) threading model, what happens when one user-level thread makes a blocking system call?
options: Only that thread blocks; the library switches to another
The whole process blocks
The kernel creates a new thread automatically to keep the others running
The call is converted to async I/O
os-process-thread:1.explanation: The kernel sees only one schedulable entity, so a blocking call stalls every user thread mapped to it. N:1 also can't use multiple cores. These limits are why early 'green thread' implementations were abandoned.

os-process-thread:1.prompt: Which threading model do Linux (NPTL) pthreads and Windows threads use?
options: M:N
os-process-thread:1.explanation: Each user thread maps to one kernel thread, so the kernel schedules them across cores and a blocking call blocks only that thread. The cost is heavier threads, since each has kernel state and a full stack.

os-process-thread:1.prompt: Go's runtime schedules many goroutines onto a small number of OS threads (bounded by GOMAXPROCS for running Go code). Which model is this?
options: M:N
Process-per-request
os-process-thread:1.explanation: Go multiplexes M goroutines onto N OS threads with its own user-space scheduler (work stealing, handoff on blocking syscalls). That gives cheap concurrency and multicore use. It's not N:1, since many OS threads run in parallel.

os-process-thread:1.prompt: What is the main advantage of user-level (N:1) threads over kernel threads?
options: They run in parallel on multiple cores
Creating and switching them needs no syscalls
A blocking syscall blocks only the calling thread, not its siblings
The kernel can preempt each one individually on a timer interrupt
os-process-thread:1.explanation: User-space switching is just saving registers in a library, which is fast. The downsides are the opposite of the other options: no parallelism, whole-process blocking, and no kernel preemption between them.

os-process-thread:1.prompt: Why is M:N threading hard to implement well, to the point that systems like Solaris and early NetBSD moved back to 1:1?
options: It can't support more than 64 threads per process
Two schedulers must cooperate on blocking and signals
It requires a GPU
It doesn't allow threads to share memory with each other
os-process-thread:1.explanation: The user-level scheduler doesn't see kernel events directly, so blocking calls, signals and priority handling need careful coordination (e.g. scheduler activations). Language runtimes like Go and Erlang manage it because they control the whole stack.

os-process-thread:1.prompt: Java 21 virtual threads mount on carrier platform threads. A virtual thread does blocking socket I/O. What happens to its carrier thread?
options: The carrier thread blocks along with it until the I/O completes
It unmounts, freeing the carrier for others
The JVM crashes
The I/O is handed to a dedicated kernel thread per virtual thread
os-process-thread:1.explanation: The JDK reimplemented blocking I/O so virtual threads park and release their carrier, giving M:N scalability with simple blocking code. Exceptions exist: in JDK 21, blocking inside synchronized blocks pins the carrier.

os-process-thread:1.prompt: How do Node.js worker_threads map onto the OS?
options: Green threads scheduled by V8 on the main thread between event-loop ticks
Real OS threads, each with its own isolate
Separate processes
Threads that share the main thread's JS heap directly
os-process-thread:1.explanation: Workers are kernel-scheduled threads, so they run JS truly in parallel, but each has its own isolate and heap; data moves by message passing or SharedArrayBuffer. They're not processes (a crash in native code still takes down the whole process).

os-process-thread:1.prompt: Which are true of the 1:1 threading model? Select all that apply.
options: Threads can run in parallel on multiple cores
A blocking syscall blocks only the calling thread
Thread creation is as cheap as a function call
Very large thread counts (e.g. 100k) are costly due to kernel structures and stacks
The kernel can't preempt individual threads
os-process-thread:1.explanation: 1:1 gives real parallelism and independent blocking at the cost of heavier threads. Creation requires a syscall and stack allocation, and the kernel schedules and preempts each thread individually.

os-process-thread:1.prompt: Which runtimes multiplex many lightweight tasks onto fewer OS threads (M:N-style)? Select all that apply.
options: Go goroutines
Erlang/Elixir BEAM processes
Java 21 virtual threads
Linux pthreads via NPTL
Plain Windows threads created with CreateThread
os-process-thread:1.explanation: Go, the BEAM VM and Java virtual threads schedule many lightweight tasks onto a pool of OS threads. NPTL pthreads and CreateThread are 1:1 kernel threads.

os-process-thread:1.prompt: With the N:1 model, a process with 8 user-level threads on an 8-core machine can run all 8 threads in parallel.
options: True
False
os-process-thread:1.explanation: False. All user threads share one kernel thread, so only one runs at a time regardless of cores. Parallelism needs multiple kernel threads (1:1 or M:N).

os-process-thread:1.prompt: In an M:N model, a user-level scheduler decides which lightweight task runs on each kernel thread, while the kernel decides which kernel thread runs on each CPU.
options: True
False
os-process-thread:1.explanation: True. Two levels of scheduling are the defining trait of M:N: the runtime maps tasks to threads, the OS maps threads to cores. That's both its power and the source of its complexity.

os-process-thread:2.prompt: A job arrives at t=2, first gets the CPU at t=5, and finishes at t=12. Its CPU burst is 4 units. What are its turnaround and response times?
options: Turnaround 10, response 3
Turnaround 12, response 5
Turnaround 7, response 3
Turnaround 10, response 6
os-process-thread:2.explanation: Turnaround = completion − arrival = 12 − 2 = 10. Response = first run − arrival = 5 − 2 = 3. Waiting time would be turnaround − burst = 6, which is the tempting mix-up in the last option.

os-process-thread:2.prompt: Which metric matters most for an interactive desktop or terminal user?
options: Throughput
Response time to first output
Total CPU utilisation across all cores and processes
Average turnaround of batch jobs
os-process-thread:2.explanation: Interactive users feel the delay before the first response, so schedulers favour short, I/O-bound tasks. Throughput and turnaround matter more for batch systems, where nobody watches individual jobs.

os-process-thread:2.prompt: A batch cluster finishes 1,800 jobs in one hour. What is its throughput?
options: 30 jobs per second
0.5 jobs per second
2 seconds per job turnaround
1,800 jobs per second
os-process-thread:2.explanation: Throughput = jobs completed / time = 1800 / 3600 s = 0.5 jobs/s. A 2 s average gap between completions doesn't tell you any individual job's turnaround, which includes its queueing time.

os-process-thread:2.prompt: Why do throughput and response time often conflict in scheduler design?
options: They're the same metric measured over different time windows
Frequent switching helps latency but costs total work
Throughput only matters on single-core machines
Response time can't be measured
os-process-thread:2.explanation: Short time slices improve responsiveness but spend more time on switching and lose cache warmth; long slices improve throughput but increase latency. Real schedulers pick a compromise per workload.

os-process-thread:2.prompt: An API's average latency is 40 ms but p99 is 2 s. Users complain. Which scheduling idea most directly targets the problem?
options: Maximise throughput by batching requests into large groups
Bound queueing so slow work can't block the rest
Increase average CPU utilisation to 100%
Use FCFS with one queue for all request types
os-process-thread:2.explanation: Tail latency comes from some requests waiting behind slow ones (a convoy). Separating or bounding slow work and fair queueing cut p99. Running at 100% utilisation makes queues, and so tail latency, explode.

os-process-thread:2.prompt: Why is running a server CPU at nearly 100% utilisation usually bad for latency?
options: CPUs overheat and throttle their clocks once they reach 100%
Waiting time grows sharply as utilisation nears 1
The OS stops scheduling at 100%
Throughput drops to zero
os-process-thread:2.explanation: In simple queueing models, mean wait scales with ρ/(1 − ρ): at 50% load waits are modest, at 95% they're about 19× the service time. Throughput is near its peak, but latency suffers, hence capacity headroom.

os-process-thread:2.prompt: Which goal means 'no process waits forever to get the CPU'?
options: Maximum throughput
Freedom from starvation
Minimum context switches, so long jobs keep their caches warm
Maximum turnaround
os-process-thread:2.explanation: Fairness and starvation freedom guarantee every runnable task eventually runs. Throughput-maximising policies like SJF can starve long jobs, which is why techniques such as aging exist.

os-process-thread:2.prompt: Which statements about scheduling metrics are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Waiting time = turnaround time − CPU burst time (ignoring I/O)
Response time is measured until the first time the job gets the CPU
Turnaround time is measured from first run to completion
Throughput is the number of jobs completed per unit of time
Lower turnaround always means higher CPU utilisation
os-process-thread:2.explanation: Turnaround is from arrival (not first run) to completion; waiting is turnaround minus service time; response is arrival to first run. Utilisation is a separate metric: an idle CPU can still give low turnaround for few jobs.

os-process-thread:2.prompt: A system runs both interactive web requests and nightly batch reports on the same machines. Which choices help both kinds of work? Select all that apply.
options: Give interactive work higher priority or a separate queue
Run batch jobs at a lower nice value / lower priority so they use spare CPU
Run everything in one FCFS queue
Use cgroups to cap the batch jobs' CPU share
Lengthen the time slice for interactive tasks so they finish without interruption
os-process-thread:2.explanation: Separating classes of work and limiting batch CPU keeps response times low while batch still uses idle capacity. One FCFS queue lets long reports block requests, and long slices hurt responsiveness rather than help.

os-process-thread:2.prompt: Minimising average waiting time and guaranteeing that no job starves are always achievable with the same scheduling policy.
options: True
False
os-process-thread:2.explanation: False. SJF/SRTF minimise average waiting but can starve long jobs if short jobs keep arriving. Adding aging or fairness costs some average performance; the goals trade off.

os-process-thread:2.prompt: For a job that never blocks on I/O, turnaround time equals its waiting time plus its CPU burst time.
options: True
False
os-process-thread:2.explanation: True. Its time in the system is spent either waiting in the ready queue or running, so turnaround = waiting + burst. With I/O, time blocked must be added too.

os-process-thread:3.prompt: Three jobs arrive at t=0 in order P1 (burst 24), P2 (3), P3 (3). Under FCFS, what is the average waiting time?
os-process-thread:3.explanation: FCFS runs P1, P2, P3: waits are 0, 24 and 27, average 51/3 = 17. Running the short jobs first (SJF) gives waits 0, 3, 6 and an average of 3, which shows the convoy effect.

os-process-thread:3.prompt: Same jobs, all at t=0: P1 (24), P2 (3), P3 (3). What is the average waiting time under non-preemptive SJF?
os-process-thread:3.explanation: SJF orders P2, P3, P1 (ties broken FCFS): waits 0, 3, 6, average 9/3 = 3. 6 is P1's individual wait, not the average.

os-process-thread:3.prompt: Jobs: P1 arrives 0 (burst 7), P2 arrives 2 (4), P3 arrives 4 (1), P4 arrives 5 (4). Under non-preemptive SJF, what is the average waiting time?
os-process-thread:3.explanation: P1 runs 0–7 (only job at t=0). At 7: P3 (1) runs 7–8, then P2 8–12 (ties with P4 broken by arrival), then P4 12–16. Waits: 0, 6, 3, 7, giving 16/4 = 4. The preemptive version (SRTF) achieves 3.

os-process-thread:3.prompt: Same jobs: P1 at 0 (7), P2 at 2 (4), P3 at 4 (1), P4 at 5 (4). Under preemptive SJF (shortest remaining time first), what is the average waiting time?
os-process-thread:3.explanation: Timeline: P1 0–2, P2 2–4, P3 4–5, P2 5–7, P4 7–11, P1 11–16. Waits: P1 9, P2 1, P3 0, P4 2, total 12, average 3. Preemption lets short arrivals jump ahead of P1's remaining 5 units.

os-process-thread:3.prompt: What is the 'convoy effect' in FCFS scheduling?
options: Short jobs pile up behind one long job
Jobs migrate between CPUs in groups to share warm caches
High-priority jobs always run first
The scheduler batches similar jobs to improve cache use
os-process-thread:3.explanation: One long job at the head of the queue holds everything up; I/O devices sit idle while short jobs wait for the CPU. It's the main weakness of FCFS. Priority-first describes priority scheduling, not the convoy effect.

os-process-thread:3.prompt: Why is pure SJF hard to implement in a real OS?
options: Sorting the ready queue on every arrival is too expensive
Next-burst length is unknown and must be estimated
SJF only works on multi-core machines
SJF requires all jobs to have equal priority
os-process-thread:3.explanation: SJF is provably optimal for average waiting time, but only with known burst lengths. Real systems predict them, e.g. τ(n+1) = α·t(n) + (1 − α)·τ(n). Sorting a ready queue is cheap.

os-process-thread:3.prompt: A low-priority task holds a lock that a high-priority task needs, while a medium-priority task keeps the CPU busy. The high-priority task is stuck. What is this called and what's the classic fix?
options: Starvation; fix it by switching to FCFS
Priority inversion; fix with priority inheritance
Deadlock; fix by killing the high-priority task
Convoy effect; fix it by shortening the time slice
os-process-thread:3.explanation: The medium task indirectly blocks the high one by starving the lock holder: priority inversion (famously on the Mars Pathfinder). Priority inheritance lets the holder run, release the lock and unblock the high task. No cycle exists, so it isn't deadlock.

os-process-thread:3.prompt: Which techniques address problems of priority scheduling? Select all that apply.
options: Aging: gradually raise the priority of tasks that have waited long
Priority inheritance for lock holders
Priority ceiling protocol
Always running the lowest-priority task first
Disabling preemption permanently
os-process-thread:3.explanation: Aging prevents starvation of low-priority tasks; priority inheritance and priority ceiling prevent priority inversion around locks. Running lowest priority first defeats the policy, and disabling preemption lets one task monopolise the CPU.

os-process-thread:3.prompt: Which statements comparing FCFS and SJF are correct? Select all that apply.
options: FCFS is simple and never starves a job
SJF minimises average waiting time for a given set of jobs available together
SJF can starve long jobs if short jobs keep arriving
FCFS is preemptive by definition
SJF needs no knowledge or estimate of burst lengths
os-process-thread:3.explanation: FCFS is fair in arrival order but suffers convoys; SJF is optimal for average wait yet starves long jobs and needs burst estimates. FCFS is non-preemptive: a job runs until it blocks or finishes.

os-process-thread:3.prompt: In a non-preemptive priority scheduler, a newly arrived high-priority job interrupts the currently running lower-priority job immediately.
options: True
False
os-process-thread:3.explanation: False. Non-preemptive means the running job keeps the CPU until it blocks or finishes; the new job is placed at the head of the ready queue. Only a preemptive priority scheduler interrupts immediately.

os-process-thread:3.prompt: If all jobs have the same CPU burst length, FCFS and non-preemptive SJF produce the same average waiting time.
options: True
False
os-process-thread:3.explanation: True. With equal bursts, SJF has nothing to reorder by length (ties are broken by arrival), so its schedule matches FCFS. SJF only helps when burst lengths differ.

os-process-thread:4.prompt: Round robin with quantum 2: P1 (burst 5) and P2 (burst 3) both arrive at t=0, P1 first. When does each finish?
options: P1 at 5, P2 at 8
P1 at 8, P2 at 7
P1 at 7, P2 at 8
P1 at 8, P2 at 5
os-process-thread:4.explanation: P1 0–2, P2 2–4, P1 4–6, P2 6–7 (done), P1 7–8 (done). So P2 finishes at 7 and P1 at 8. 'P1 at 5, P2 at 8' is the FCFS answer.

os-process-thread:4.prompt: Round robin, quantum 4: P1 (24), P2 (3), P3 (3), all at t=0 in that order. What is the average waiting time?
options: About 5.67
About 7.33
os-process-thread:4.explanation: P1 0–4, P2 4–7, P3 7–10, then P1 10–30. Waits: P1 30 − 24 = 6, P2 4, P3 7, total 17, average 17/3 ≈ 5.67. 17 is the FCFS average (and the total here), a tempting slip.

os-process-thread:4.prompt: What happens to round robin as the time quantum becomes very large (larger than every burst)?
options: It becomes SJF
It degenerates into FCFS
It becomes priority scheduling
It stops preempting I/O-bound jobs only
os-process-thread:4.explanation: If no job ever exhausts its quantum, each runs to completion in queue order: that's FCFS. A very small quantum goes the other way, approaching processor sharing but with heavy switching overhead.

os-process-thread:4.prompt: Why is round robin usually better than FCFS for interactive systems?
options: It always gives a lower average turnaround time than FCFS
A ready job gets a turn within about (n − 1) × quantum
It never context-switches
It requires knowing burst lengths
os-process-thread:4.explanation: RR's strength is response time: no job waits behind a long one for more than a bounded time. Its average turnaround can actually be worse than FCFS or SJF, especially when bursts are similar.

os-process-thread:4.prompt: In a multilevel feedback queue (MLFQ), a job uses its entire time allotment at the top priority level. What usually happens?
options: It is promoted to an even higher level as a reward
It is demoted to a lower queue
It is terminated
It stays at the same level, because MLFQ never moves running jobs
os-process-thread:4.explanation: MLFQ learns from behaviour: jobs that burn their full allotment are treated as CPU-bound and moved down, while jobs that block early (interactive, I/O-bound) stay high. That approximates SJF without knowing burst lengths.

os-process-thread:4.prompt: Why does MLFQ periodically boost all jobs back to the top queue?
options: To reduce memory used by the queues
To stop starvation and re-rank changed jobs
To force all jobs into FCFS order
To make CPU-bound jobs finish before interactive ones arrive
os-process-thread:4.explanation: Without a boost, a steady stream of interactive jobs could starve CPU-bound jobs in low queues forever, and a job that turned interactive would stay stuck low. The boost period is a tuning knob between fairness and responsiveness.

os-process-thread:4.prompt: A program games an MLFQ scheduler by issuing a tiny I/O just before its quantum expires, so it stays at top priority while using most of the CPU. What's the standard fix?
options: Make the quantum longer so yielding early gains nothing
Track total CPU per level, regardless of yields
Ban I/O for CPU-bound programs
Switch to FCFS
os-process-thread:4.explanation: Tracking cumulative CPU time per level (rather than resetting on each yield) removes the incentive to yield early. Longer quanta don't fix gaming; they just change when the trick is needed.

os-process-thread:4.prompt: Which statements about choosing a round-robin quantum are correct? Select all that apply.
options: It should be large relative to context-switch cost, or overhead dominates
Too large a quantum hurts response time
A quantum slightly longer than a typical interactive burst lets those jobs finish in one slice
The quantum must equal the average burst length exactly
A smaller quantum always increases throughput
os-process-thread:4.explanation: Quantum choice balances switching overhead against responsiveness; letting typical short bursts complete in one slice works well. There's no 'exactly the average' rule, and tiny quanta reduce throughput because of overhead.

os-process-thread:4.prompt: Which are core rules of a typical MLFQ scheduler? Select all that apply.
options: Higher-priority queues run before lower ones
Jobs in the same queue are scheduled round robin
New jobs start at the highest priority
Jobs never move between queues
Lower queues often get longer time quanta
os-process-thread:4.explanation: MLFQ runs higher queues first, round-robins within a queue, starts new jobs high and gives lower (CPU-bound) queues longer slices to reduce switching. Movement between queues is the 'feedback' in its name.

os-process-thread:4.prompt: Round robin always gives a lower average turnaround time than FCFS.
options: True
False
os-process-thread:4.explanation: False. With equal-length jobs, RR interleaves them so they all finish near the end, making average turnaround worse than FCFS. RR's benefit is response time, not turnaround.

os-process-thread:4.prompt: MLFQ tends to favour I/O-bound, interactive jobs without needing to know burst lengths in advance.
options: True
False
os-process-thread:4.explanation: True. Jobs that block before using their allotment stay in high-priority queues, so the scheduler infers 'short burst' from observed behaviour instead of needing predictions like pure SJF.

os-process-thread:5.prompt: On modern hardware, roughly what order of magnitude is the direct cost of a thread context switch on Linux?
options: Nanoseconds (about 1–10 ns)
Microseconds (about 1–10 µs)
Milliseconds (about 10–100 ms)
Seconds
os-process-thread:5.explanation: Saving and restoring state plus scheduler work takes on the order of microseconds. The indirect cost of cold caches and TLB misses afterwards can exceed that. Milliseconds is the scale of time slices, not of the switch itself.

os-process-thread:5.prompt: What is usually the biggest hidden cost of frequent context switches?
options: The kernel writing each PCB out to disk on every switch
Cache and TLB pollution
Recompiling the program
Network packets being dropped while the CPU is busy switching
os-process-thread:5.explanation: After a switch, the CPU caches hold the previous thread's data, so the new thread takes many cache misses. That indirect cost often dwarfs the few microseconds of direct switching. PCBs stay in memory.

os-process-thread:5.prompt: A thread-per-request Java service handles 5,000 concurrent slow requests with 5,000 threads, and CPU shows high system time. What's the most likely explanation?
options: The JIT compiler is disabled
Thousands of threads: switching and stack overhead
The garbage collector runs too often because of short-lived objects
TCP keepalive is disabled
os-process-thread:5.explanation: Thousands of kernel threads mean lots of switching and kernel bookkeeping (system time) and large stack reservations. Event loops (Node, Netty) or virtual threads handle the same concurrency with far fewer OS threads.

os-process-thread:5.prompt: For a purely CPU-bound task pool on an 8-core machine, what thread count is usually best?
options: About 8 (one per core)
About 800
1, to avoid switching
As many as there are tasks
os-process-thread:5.explanation: CPU-bound threads beyond the core count just take turns, adding switches without adding throughput. One thread wastes 7 cores. I/O-bound pools can be larger, since threads spend time blocked.

os-process-thread:5.prompt: How do PCID (x86) or ASID (Arm) tags reduce the cost of switching between processes?
options: They make the CPU clock faster
TLB entries are tagged, so no full flush
They disable virtual memory for trusted processes to skip translation
They let two processes share one stack
os-process-thread:5.explanation: Without tags, changing page tables would flush the TLB and every following access would miss. Tags let entries from several address spaces coexist, which became more important after KPTI (Meltdown mitigation) increased page-table switching.

os-process-thread:5.prompt: Why is an event loop (like Node.js) cheaper than thread-per-connection for 50k mostly idle connections, in terms of switching?
options: Event loops run on faster, dedicated CPU cores
No kernel thread per connection to switch between
Event loops don't use the kernel at all, so there are no syscalls
Threads can't handle more than 1,000 connections
os-process-thread:5.explanation: The event loop switches between connections in user space with a function call, and the kernel reports only ready sockets. The kernel is still involved (epoll, syscalls); there's just no thread per connection to schedule.

os-process-thread:5.prompt: A low-latency trading process busy-polls a network queue on an isolated core instead of blocking. Why accept 100% CPU on that core?
options: Blocking calls are not supported on Linux for network queues
It avoids wakeup switches and their jitter
Busy-polling saves power
It deliberately increases cache misses on other cores
os-process-thread:5.explanation: Blocking means a wakeup, a context switch and cold caches on every message, adding microseconds and variance. Spinning on a dedicated core keeps the thread hot. It wastes CPU, so it only makes sense when latency is worth it.

os-process-thread:5.prompt: Which design choices reduce context-switch overhead in a backend service? Select all that apply.
options: Size CPU-bound thread pools near the core count
Use async I/O or an event loop instead of a thread per blocked connection
Batch small work items so each wakeup does more work
Spawn a new OS thread for every incoming request
Use very fine-grained locks that threads frequently block on
os-process-thread:5.explanation: Fewer runnable threads, non-blocking I/O and batching all reduce how often the scheduler switches. Thread-per-request and lock contention that forces frequent blocking both increase switches.

os-process-thread:5.prompt: `pidstat -w` shows a service with very high voluntary context switches per second. Which are plausible causes? Select all that apply.
options: Threads frequently blocking on contended locks
Many small blocking I/O calls (e.g. unbuffered tiny writes)
Threads sleeping and waking in tight polling loops with short sleeps
The process being CPU-bound and preempted by the timer
Too few runnable threads to fill the cores
os-process-thread:5.explanation: Voluntary switches mean the thread chose to wait: lock contention, small blocking I/O or short sleeps. Timer preemption of CPU-bound work shows up as involuntary switches, and having few runnable threads doesn't in itself cause switching.

os-process-thread:5.prompt: Switching between two coroutines or async tasks in the same thread usually costs much less than an OS thread context switch, because it doesn't enter the kernel.
options: True
False
os-process-thread:5.explanation: True. A user-space switch is roughly a function call plus saving a little state, with no syscall, scheduler run or address-space change. That's why event loops and green threads scale to huge concurrency.

os-process-thread:5.prompt: Adding more threads to a CPU-bound workload always increases throughput, as long as there's enough RAM for their stacks.
options: True
False
os-process-thread:5.explanation: False. Past the number of cores, extra CPU-bound threads only add context switches and cache contention, so throughput flattens or drops. RAM isn't the limiting factor here; the cores are.
